newsitem.title: CANADA: Martin introduces Canada Pension Plan reform.
newsitem.headline: Martin introduces Canada Pension Plan reform.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin introduced legislation to Parliament on Friday that he said would secure the future of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
"It is my privilege to table draft legislation that secures the future of the Canada Pension Plan," Martin told the House of Commons, Parliament's elected chamber.

He said the CPP would move from a pay-as-you-go to fuller funding that would provide for benefits as Canada's population ages, by raising premium rates to 9.9 percent of insurable earnings over the next six years from 5.85 percent now.
Martin, a Liberal, said he now had support from all provinces except British Columbia and Saskatchewan.
The two provinces have New Democratic Party governments but are not able to block the reforms now that Conservative-run Ontario has come on board.

Martin said the chief actuary of the government-run plan had warned that without increases the fund would run out of money in less than 20 years and without quick action premiums would have had to be raised to more than 14 percent.
The premiums are paid equally by employer and employee.
Without action now, he said, younger generations would have to pay more than twice as much as they do at present without getting any more for it.
"This is not fair. This is not affordable," he said.

Adressing opposition Reform Party members of Parliament, who have suggested allowing Canadians to manage their own retirement funds, Martin said neither Ottawa nor the public wanted to dismantle the CPP.
He said all benefits would remain fully indexed to inflation. The changes will not affect retired pensioners or those over the age of 65 as of the end of 1997.
The ages of retirement under the plan remain unchanged, Martin added.
He said that during consultations across the country, Canadians had asked that governments no longer have exclusive access to those CPP funds that have not been disbursed.
"We've done that. Governments have agreed to limit their access and to pay interest at market rates," he said.
Martin said that with the exception of a small additional increase in the contribution rate for 1997, the proposed changes would come into effect in 1998.
Martin asserted that "almost no other industrialized country has done as much as Canada to come to grips with the problems of an ageing population and increasing longevity."

Currently the CPP has a reserve fund equal to only two years of benefits, and this is declining, Martin said. The new arrangements would provide for this fund to grow to five years' worth of benefits.
